title: Jobs indicator shows up when used with zoxide
body:
<!--
─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Please run the following command to create an issue:

  starship bug-report

  An issue will be pre-populated with your system's configuration,
  making the process a whole lot quicker 😊
─────────────────────────────────────────────
-->

## Bug Report

#### Current Behavior

When [zoxide](https://github.com/reporter/zoxide) and starship are initialized together, like so:

```sh
eval "$(starship init bash)"
eval "$(zoxide init bash)"
```

The indicator (✦) shows up when changing directory, even when no jobs in the background. It disappears when you issue other commands or press enter.

However, if you swap the order of initialization:

```sh
eval "$(zoxide init bash)"
eval "$(starship init bash)"
```

It works fine.

#### Expected Behavior

zoxide does not spawn any background commands, so the indicator should not be showing background jobs. Order of initialization should not matter as these are two unrelated tools.

#### Additional context/Screenshots

Original issue: https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/4858

I'm the author of zoxide, I'd be happy to provide any necessary context to help with debugging.

#### Environment

- Starship version: 1.12.0
- Shell type: bash
- Shell version: 5.1.16
- Terminal emulator: xfce4-terminal
- Operating system: Arch Linux

#### Relevant Shell Configuration
<!--
  Based on the shell you use, please paste the appropriate configuration.
  The default location for your shell is:
    Bash: ~/.bashrc

-->

```sh
[[ $- != *i* ]] && return
source /usr/share/fzf/completion.bash
source /usr/share/fzf/key-bindings.bash
bind "set completion-ignore-case on"
shopt -s histappend
shopt -s extglob
eval "$(starship init bash)"
eval "$(zoxide init bash)"
export HISTCONTROL=erasedups:ignoreboth
export HISTFILESIZE=10000
export HISTSIZE=10000
```

#### Starship Configuration
<!-- Can be found in  ~/.config/starship.toml -->

```toml

format = "$directory$git_branch$git_status$cmd_duration$jobs"

[character]
disabled = true

[cmd_duration]

[directory]

```

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
I use only zoxide as part of my own overengineered bashrc and I'm seeing the same problem. 

I use `jobs -l` in my function for PROMPT_COMMAND and every time I change directory I see:
```
[1]  3955696 Done                    \command zoxide add -- "${__zoxide_oldpwd}"
```

I just took the "quick & dirty" solution of grepping it out with `jobs -l | grep -v zoxide` but IMHO there is something going on with zoxide and bg jobs.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> IMHO there is something going on with zoxide and bg jobs.

As mentioned by @participant2, the hook used by zoxide to update the scores when the current directory is changed registers as a background job. I'm not sure why changing the order of initialization fixes it, which is why I created this issue here to see if we could arrive at a more reliable solution.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
> I'm not sure why changing the order of initialization fixes it

Could it just be that perhaps executing zoxide first gives enough time for the hook to be done and not being detected by starship?

I experimented putting a `sleep 1` just before my `jobs -l` and I see:
```
[1]  3492748 Done                    sleep 1
```
No sign of zoxide task anymore. This happens even without zoxide installed. 

Sorry for my ignorance, but perhaps there is a special behavior from bash side in relation with PROMPT_COMMAND? Are you hooking your function with this bash feature?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: zoxide prepends its hook to `$PROMPT_COMMAND`, which is why it's getting run before the `jobs` command. We need to check how Starship avoids overriding hooks in `$PROMPT_COMMAND`, that should tell us why it is dependent on order of initialization.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
@reporter This init problem has been a huge thorn in our side for a long time. The last time we did a major restructuring of the bash init script, I posted [a comment](https://github.com/starship/starship/pull/1185#issuecomment-641721907) which basically said that if [the current] system didn't fix it, I'm not sure anything would, aside from a dedicated preexec framework.

Anyways, the way starship currently works is that if there is another `PROMPT_COMMAND` registered, it [grabs the command and stores it into another string, and installs our own `PROMPT_COMMAND`](https://github.com/starship/starship/blob/master/src/init/starship.bash#LL92C1-L99C7). Then, while running `starship_precmd()`, it will [`eval` the saved string](https://github.com/starship/starship/blob/master/src/init/starship.bash#LL52C1-L53C38).

When starship is initialized after zoxide, starship will look for jobs, then fire the zoxide hook, meaning that zoxide jobs never show up in the background jobs count (since starship has already counted background jobs before starting zoxide).

When zoxide is initialized after starship, bash will evaluate the zoxide hook, then move to evaluate starship_precmd. Now, in most cases, frameworks that run hooks like this will background them, but it doesn't look like zoxide does this? If it doesn't background anything in the bash script, I'm as confused as you are as to why there's a background job showing up.

This is a general problem with bash for most frameworks that need to hook `PROMPT_COMMAND`: many frameworks will background their jobs to reduce latency, but if those jobs are run before `starship_precmd`, we have no way of telling whether this is a user-started job that's running in the background between prompt draws, or a short-term job run by a framework that's likely to terminate shortly after the prompt draw finishes. I'm not even sure there's a principled way to tell, short of a framework that lets you register function invocations for `PROMPT_COMMAND` and then removes those jobs from the job listing before counting.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant5 thank you for the detailed response. This seems to be related to the way subshells are executed in Bash:

```bash
# prints `Done    /bin/echo`.
echo $(/bin/echo; jobs -l)

# No output.
/bin/echo; jobs -l
```

Is there a reason why we don't use `jobs -r` to only see currently running jobs?

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
Interesting. Does this imply that `PROMPT_COMMAND`s are executed in a subshell? I'd be surprised by this, since the `jobs` call in `starship_precmd` has access to the jobs that the user is currently running, and I would expect it to be limited to the jobs of the subshell if this is the case. I know very little of how jobs interact with subshells--if you know something about this, or could point me to a good reference, I'd appreciate it.

* * *

The idea of the jobs indicator is to indicate whether there are jobs in the background, not necessarily what's running. As a simple example, if I run `sleep 10` and then Ctrl+Z, there are no jobs *running* (indeed, `jobs -r` is empty), but if I then attempt to Ctrl+D out, I'm warned that there are stopped jobs. I would consider if confusing if the prompt is telling me there are no jobs, but the shell is saying otherwise.

I'm not *fundamentally* opposed to changing the behavior, but

1. I believe the current behavior is the default for most bash-compatible prompts (haven't looked recently)
2. This would need to be a breaking change since it changes the semantic meaning of a symbol in the prompt
3. I don't think this solves the more general problem of if the `PROMPT_COMMAND` hook launches a background job, as those may still be running when the starship hook fires (in particular, I seem to recall that `z.sh` is affected by this).

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> The idea of the jobs indicator is to indicate whether there are jobs in the background, not necessarily what's running.

Fair enough, but jobs marked as `Done` would not stop the shell from exiting. Perhaps they could be filtered out?

> Does this imply that PROMPT_COMMANDs are executed in a subshell?

Nope. `PROMPT_COMMAND` can change environment variables, current directory, etc - a privilege that subshells do not have. However, subshells do have access to parent `jobs`.

---

This issue only seems to happen when launching an external process. I did find two hacks that seem to fix the problem:

```bash
# Problematic - prints `Done    /bin/echo` at every prompt.
PROMPT_COMMAND='/bin/echo; jobs -l'

# No output.
PROMPT_COMMAND='/bin/echo & wait $!; jobs -l'

# No output.
PROMPT_COMMAND='"$(/bin/echo > /dev/null)"; jobs -l'
```

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
Filtering on the output of jobs is an interesting idea, but I prefer solutions that involve minimal output parsing where possible.

I am unable to find any sort of documentation on the output of `jobs` for bash, but the POSIX man page claims that the only valid states for jobs are running, stopped, done, and some unspecified output for a job which was terminated by a signal.

Since we want to select jobs which are not terminated, I think we can just do two loops over the running and stopped jobs. So instead of this:

```
for job in $(jobs -p); do [[ $job ]] && ((NUM_JOBS++)); done   # Count all jobs
```

we can do this:

```
for job in $(jobs -pr); do [[ $job ]] && ((NUM_JOBS++)); done  # Count running jobs
for job in $(jobs -ps); do [[ $job ]] && ((NUM_JOBS++)); done  # Count stopped jobs
```

This does incur an extra subshell spawn, but it seems like it works on my system to avoid counting done/signaled jobs. (There should also be a principled way of avoiding the subshell spawns since `jobs` is a builtin, but frankly I doubt it matters all that much).

I guess the question that remains is whether anyone considers done/signaled jobs to be part of their background job count.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Actually, just running `jobs` once and discarding the output will remove the `Done` jobs. So this works just as well:

```
jobs &> /dev/null
for job in $(jobs -p); do [[ $job ]] && ((NUM_JOBS++)); done   # Count all jobs
```

> I guess the question that remains is whether anyone considers done/signaled jobs to be part of their background job count.

IMO, we should not count `Done` jobs:

- As I showed above, running the `jobs` command once removes all `Done` jobs, so the current behavior is that the user sees the background job indicator on one prompt, and then it goes away on the next prompt - I think this is confusing / inconsistent
- If the job is finished executing, it doesn't really fit the definition of a running background task. Quoting from https://starship.rs/config/#jobs (emphasis mine)
  > The `jobs` module shows the current number of jobs **running**.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Apparently, this behavior is caused by a bug in Bash 5.2, but has been fixed since:

- https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-bash/2022-07/msg00117.html
- https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-bash/2022-09/msg00067.html

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
Awesome! The patch has not made it into the latest point release of bash yet (currently 5.2.9) so I suspect it'll be quite some time before it's generally available to most bash users. Given that, I think it would be best if we patched this (we were making efforts to support users on Scientific Linux 6 up until last year, and that thing was shipping software from 2009).

The delta you suggested with calling jobs and redirecting to devnull works for me. Would you mind submitting a PR with that line and a comment explaining why it's necessary, and I'll approve it?
